Trademark Refusal Review in China: The 15-Day Deadline and How to Respond

A refusal is not the end of an application, but it does start a short clock. Under the revised law the request for review is due in 15 days, while a Madrid designation runs on a separate 15-day or 30-day timetable counted from the WIPO notification.

Two Clocks: The Domestic 15 Days and the Madrid Route

A refusal is not the end of an application, but it does start a clock. Under Article 37 of the revised Trademark Law, an applicant dissatisfied with a refusal may request review within 15 days; CNIPA then decides the review within nine months, extendable by three months. Miss the 15 days and the refusal becomes final on the original application, so the first job is calendaring, not advocacy.

International registrations designating China run on a different and easily confused timetable. When WIPO notifies a provisional refusal, the period for requesting review is counted from the date the holder receives that notification: 15 days for a refusal issued ex officio and 30 days for a refusal based on an opposition. These figures come from WIPO's official time-limits table and its Information Notice No. 19 of 2011. Do not assume the domestic rule and the Madrid periods are the same instrument; identify which refusal you have before computing the date.

RouteTriggerPeriod to request review
Chinese national application (Art. 37)Receipt of the refusal15 days
Madrid designation, ex officio refusalHolder receives the WIPO notification of provisional refusal15 days
Madrid designation, opposition-based refusalHolder receives the WIPO notification of provisional refusal30 days

What Happens After You File

Once a review request is filed, the case is examined on its merits and on the evidence submitted with it. CNIPA's decision on a refusal review is due within nine months, extendable by three months under Article 37; those are decision targets for the authority, not deadlines for you to fill. Your evidence deadline is the one to watch: supplementary evidence in a Madrid-related review is to be submitted within three months from the date the review request is filed, per WIPO's time-limits materials.

That structure rewards preparation. A review request that says only that the marks are different wastes the best opportunity to put the full case on record. Where the refusal cites earlier marks, decide early whether you are arguing dissimilarity of the signs, dissimilarity of the goods or services, both, or a coexistence-based position supported by use. The chosen theory determines what evidence to gather in the weeks after filing.

Calendar three things separately: the deadline to request review, the deadline for supplementary evidence, and the date on which a decision is expected. They run from different starting points and confusing them is a common, avoidable loss.

The Six-Argument Menu

Practitioner guidance converges on six responses to a Chinese refusal. Most cases use more than one.

  1. Argue the signs and the goods. Submit a structured comparison showing the applied-for mark is not similar to the cited mark, or that the designated goods or services are not similar, with reference to the relevant sub-classes.
  2. Rely on coexistence or acquired distinctiveness. Put in evidence of honest concurrent use, market recognition, or distinctiveness acquired through use, so that confusion is unlikely.
  3. Attack the citation. Where the cited registration has not been used for three consecutive years, consider a non-use cancellation action to remove the obstacle at its source.
  4. Obtain a letter of consent. A coexistence agreement or consent from the earlier rights holder can resolve a citation that argument alone cannot.
  5. Accept a partial refusal. Where only some goods are blocked, consider narrowing the designation to preserve a filing date for the acceptable items.
  6. File a parallel Chinese national application. For a Madrid designation, a direct national filing can keep protection moving independently while the international refusal is contested.

Building the Evidence File

A review is won on documents. Keep any coexistence or consent document properly executed and translated, and make sure it identifies the exact marks and goods at issue. For acquired distinctiveness, assemble dated advertising, sales records, marketplace listings, media coverage and distribution materials showing that the applied-for sign identifies your business in China, not merely that it exists.

For a non-use cancellation against a cited mark, the evidence question is different: the issue is whether the earlier registration has been genuinely used on the designated goods, so preserve the filing date, the three-year window counted back from it, and the goods on which use must be shown. A cancellation and a refusal review are separate proceedings; coordinate them so the review record reflects the cancellation's status.

Keep a single indexed file: the refusal notice, the WIPO notification where relevant, the review request, every exhibit, and a dated log of submissions. If the matter later moves to an appeal or a court, that chronology is the spine of the case. For the common grounds behind refusals, see common reasons for rejection in China.

A Madrid-Specific Playbook

For holders who entered China through the Madrid System, the most useful protective step is often a parallel Chinese national application. It creates an independent right that is not hostage to the fate of the international designation, and it allows a narrowed or divided filing strategy that the international registration cannot accommodate. Discuss with counsel whether the national application should claim the same scope, a reduced list of goods, or a separate Chinese-character mark.

Partial refusals deserve a deliberate decision rather than a reflex appeal. Where the objection is confined to part of the designation, accepting a narrower scope may preserve an early filing date for the rest while a fuller case is built. Conversely, where the blocked goods are commercially central, a parallel filing combined with a cancellation against the citation may be worth the extra work.

The WIPO notification starts the clock. Make sure the holder's address on record is monitored and that the notification date is logged the day it arrives. A 15-day or 30-day period leaves no room to reconstruct authority, translations and evidence from scratch, so authorise local counsel before a refusal is ever issued.

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: Article 37 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (adopted 26 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027); WIPO, official time limits for responding to provisional refusals in designated contracting parties; WIPO Information Notice No. 19 of 2011. The Madrid periods are counted from the holder's receipt of the WIPO notification and differ between ex officio and opposition-based refusals; confirm the current WIPO table and the official announcements and rules with your agent. This is general information, not legal advice.
